text: 1. Overview — The Spine as a System

body: The spine has to do two incompatible things at once: protect the neural tissue running through it and stay mobile enough to be useful. It resolves that by stacking many small joints, each moving a little, so the column as a whole moves a great deal while no single segment is very mobile.

That design produces the two great families of spinal pathology: too much motion at one segment (instability, spondylolisthesis, segmental pain) and too little space for the neural structures (stenosis, radiculopathy, myelopathy).

• 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 (usually fused) coccygeal.
  • 23 intervertebral discs. There is no disc between C1 and C2, and none above C1 — so the first disc is C2–C3 and the last is L5–S1.
  • Discs make up roughly 20–33% of the height of the vertebral column, which is why we lose height with age and are measurably shorter at the end of the day.

rows: Secondary — develops with standing and walking (~12–18 months)

body:
• Primary curves are kyphotic and follow the shape of the fetal spine. Secondary curves are lordotic and are acquired as the child lifts the head and then stands.
  • The curves act as a spring. A curved column resists axial compression far better than a straight one, and the alternating curves let the spine absorb load rather than transmit it rigidly to the head.

text: 1.2.1 Sagittal balance — the parameters you will see on reports

body:
• Sagittal vertical axis (SVA) — a plumb line from C7 should fall within about 5 cm of the posterosuperior corner of S1.
  • Pelvic incidence (PI) — a fixed, individual morphological value: PI = pelvic tilt + sacral slope. It does not change with position.
  • PI – LL mismatch — lumbar lordosis should roughly match pelvic incidence; a mismatch greater than about 10° is associated with pain and disability.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Sagittal balance is the single most useful concept to take from spinal surgery into rehabilitation. A patient whose trunk has drifted forward must work continuously with the hip extensors and the posterior chain simply to stand upright — which is exhausting, and is a common but under-recognised cause of “I can walk only a short distance.”
Look for the compensations rather than the number: pelvic retroversion, knee flexion, reduced thoracic kyphosis and a forward head. When a patient describes needing to lean on a trolley, ask whether they lean because of claudication (stenosis, relieved by flexion) or because of sagittal imbalance (fatigue, relieved by support). The management differs.

body: The smallest piece of spine that behaves like a spine: two adjacent vertebrae, the disc between them, the two facet joints, and the connecting ligaments.

• This gives the three-joint complex: one disc anteriorly and two facet joints posteriorly. They are mechanically coupled — degeneration in one loads the others, which is why disc height loss and facet arthropathy travel together.
  • Load sharing: in neutral standing the anterior column (body and disc) carries roughly 80% of axial load and the facets about 20%. In extension the facet share rises substantially — one reason extension-based pain suggests a posterior element source.

label: Memory aid
text: Anterior column = the shock absorber. Posterior column = the guide rail. The disc takes the load; the facets decide which directions the segment is allowed to move in. Most of the regional differences in the spine are differences in the orientation of that guide rail.

rows: All directions — the most mobile region
Fracture (least space for the cord), scoliosis

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Facet orientation explains almost every regional difference. Sagittal lumbar facets permit flexion and extension but block rotation — which is why the lumbar spine tolerates bending but is injured by twisting, and why rotation is only about 2° per segment in the lumbar spine.
Coronal thoracic facets permit rotation but the ribs restrict everything else — which is why the thoracic spine is the stiff middle of the column and why thoracic pain deserves more suspicion than lumbar pain: it is less often mechanical.

body:
• Disc pressure varies greatly with posture. Relative to standing (100%), it is lowest lying supine, higher sitting, and highest in forward flexion while lifting.
  • The classical Nachemson figures have been refined by later in-vivo measurements, but the ranking has held: lying < standing < sitting < flexed < flexed and loaded.
  • Intradiscal pressure also rises through the day and falls overnight as the disc rehydrates.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
The practical advice that follows from disc pressure is about position, not about avoiding load. Discs need loading and unloading cycles to be nourished (see 3.2). The message is to vary posture frequently and to avoid sustained loaded flexion, not to avoid bending altogether.
One concrete implication: disc pressure and hydration are highest in the morning, so heavy flexion-based loading in the first hour after rising is the worst time for a vulnerable disc.

body:
• Body — anterior, weight-bearing, increasing in size as you descend.
  • Pedicles — short, strong bridges from body to posterior elements. They are the strongest part of the vertebra and the anchor point for surgical screws.
  • Laminae — form the roof of the canal; the target of laminectomy.
  • Spinous process — posterior, palpable, a lever for the extensor muscles.
  • Transverse processes — lateral levers for rotation and side-bending.
  • Superior and inferior articular processes — carry the facets and determine the segment’s permitted motion.
  • Vertebral foramen — which, stacked, forms the spinal canal.

• Small, broad body with uncinate processes projecting upward from the lateral margins, forming the uncovertebral joints (of Luschka).
  • Transverse foramen in each transverse process. The vertebral artery enters at C6 in most people and ascends to C1 — it does not traverse the C7 foramen.
  • Large triangular vertebral foramen — more room for the cord than anywhere else, which is why cervical stenosis must be marked before it becomes symptomatic.
  • Bifid spinous processes at C3–C6.
  • Facets oriented about 45° from horizontal, allowing flexion, extension, rotation and lateral flexion — but also making the cervical spine the most mobile and least protected region.

• Atlas — a ring with no body and no spinous process. Two lateral masses, an anterior and a posterior arch, and a groove on the posterior arch for the vertebral artery.
  • Axis — carries the dens (odontoid process), which is effectively the body of the atlas fused to C2. It is held against the anterior arch of C1 by the transverse ligament.
  • Atlanto-occipital joint — flexion and extension: the “yes” joint. Roughly 50% of cervical flexion/extension.
  • Atlanto-axial joint — rotation: the “no” joint. Roughly 50% of total cervical rotation, about 45° to each side.

• Vertebra prominens — long, non-bifid spinous process; the standard surface landmark.
  • Its transverse foramen, when present, transmits only small veins — not the vertebral artery.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
The atlanto-dental interval (ADI) — the gap between the anterior arch of C1 and the dens — should be under 3 mm in adults and under about 5 mm in children.
Widening means transverse ligament incompetence and atlantoaxial instability. The groups to think of are rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome, and it matters enormously before any procedure involving neck positioning or intubation. In a rheumatoid patient with new neck pain or any long-tract sign, image the craniocervical junction before manual therapy or manipulation.

body:
• Heart-shaped bodies with costal demifacets on the posterolateral body for the rib heads, and facets on the transverse processes for the rib tubercles (ribs 1–10).
  • Long, downward-angled spinous processes that overlap like roof tiles — which is why the palpable spinous process often lies opposite the body of the vertebra below.
  • Coronally oriented facets favour rotation, but the rib cage restricts overall motion, making this the stiffest region.
  • The smallest vertebral canal relative to cord size — the cord has least room to escape here.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Two reasons to take thoracic symptoms more seriously than lumbar ones.
First, the canal is narrowest and the cord blood supply is most tenuous here (the T4–T9 watershed), so thoracic cord compression can progress quickly and with little warning.
Second, mechanical thoracic pain is less common than in the neck or low back, so the prior probability of a non-mechanical cause — fracture, metastasis, infection, or referred visceral pain — is higher. New thoracic pain in an older patient, or with any systemic feature, deserves imaging rather than a course of treatment.

body:
• Large kidney-shaped bodies built for load.
  • Sagittally oriented facets — permitting flexion and extension freely, but restricting rotation to about 2° per segment.
  • Mammillary and accessory processes — small bony prominences at the junction of the superior articular and transverse processes. Clinically important because the medial branch of the dorsal ramus runs in the groove between them, held by the mamillo-accessory ligament — this is the target for medial branch blocks.
  • Pars interarticularis — the bone between the superior and inferior articular processes. It is the stress riser of the lumbar spine.
  • At L5–S1 the facets become more coronally oriented, which allows more rotation but provides less resistance to forward translation.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Spondylolysis is a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis, most often at L5. It is produced by repeated extension and rotation — hence its frequency in gymnasts, cricketers, dancers, throwers and rowers.
In an adolescent athlete with extension-related low back pain, this is the diagnosis to exclude. Plain films are insensitive; MRI with STIR detects the pre-fracture stress reaction, which is the stage at which relative rest actually works.
If the pars fails bilaterally, the vertebra can translate forward — isthmic spondylolisthesis. Contrast this with degenerative spondylolisthesis, which occurs at L4–L5 in older patients with intact pars but incompetent facets and disc.

body:
• Five fused sacral vertebrae forming a wedge that transmits load from the spine to the pelvis.
  • Sacral promontory — the anterior projecting edge of S1; an obstetric and surgical landmark.
  • Auricular surface — the articulation with the ilium at the sacroiliac joint.
  • Anterior and posterior sacral foramina — transmitting the ventral and dorsal rami of the sacral nerves.
  • Sacral hiatus — the defect at the lower end from failure of the S5 laminae to fuse, bounded by the sacral cornua. This is the access point for caudal epidural injection.
  • Coccyx — usually four fused segments; attachment for the pelvic floor and the coccygeal ligaments. Relevant in coccydynia.
• Lumbosacral transitional vertebrae are common — present in roughly 10–20% of people: a sacralised L5 or a lumbarised S1.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Transitional vertebrae are a real source of clinical error. If the radiologist and the clinician number the segments differently, an injection or an operation can be performed at the wrong level.
Whenever a transitional segment is present, count from a fixed reference and state the convention used — and confirm the level against the report before any procedure. Bertolotti syndrome describes pain attributed to an enlarged transverse process articulating with the sacrum, and remains a contested diagnosis.

rows: A notochordal remnant. 70–90% water in youth, rich in proteoglycans, with loose type II collagen
Behaves as an incompressible gel — converts axial load into radial pressure on the annulus
15–25 concentric lamellae of type I collagen, fibres angled ~60° from vertical and alternating direction in successive layers
Contains the nucleus. The alternating angle means only half the fibres resist rotation in any one direction
Hyaline cartilage covering the vertebral body surfaces
The route of nutrition for the disc, and the usual site of initial failure

label: Memory aid
text: The disc is a water balloon in a radial-ply tyre. Load the balloon and it pushes outward on the tyre walls. Twist it, and only half the plies are aligned to resist — which is why rotation is the movement that damages the annulus, and why the sagittal lumbar facets exist to prevent it.

body:
• Blood vessels regress from the disc through childhood. After about age 8 it is avascular — the largest avascular structure in the body.
  • Nutrition is by diffusion through the cartilaginous endplates, and that diffusion is driven by loading and unloading cycles which pump fluid in and out.
  • Consequences: immobility starves the disc, and endplate sclerosis (from ageing, smoking, or vibration) blocks the supply route.
  • Degeneration begins with proteoglycan loss → reduced water content → the nucleus can no longer pressurise → load is transferred to the annulus and the facets → disc height falls → the facets subluxate and the foramen narrows.

• Only the outer third of the annulus is innervated, by the sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerve, which arises from the ventral ramus and the grey ramus communicans and re-enters the foramen.
  • The sinuvertebral nerve also supplies the PLL, the anterior dura and the epidural vessels — and it supplies more than one level, which is part of why discogenic pain is so poorly localised.
  • In degeneration, nerve and vessel ingrowth extends deeper into the annulus and even into the nucleus — the anatomical basis for a previously insensate structure becoming painful.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
“The disc needs movement to eat.” That single sentence justifies most of what a physiatrist advises: early mobilisation rather than bed rest, frequent postural change rather than one “correct” posture, and graded loading rather than avoidance.
It also explains why prolonged sitting and whole-body vibration are genuine risk factors — both represent sustained static loading with no pumping cycle.

body:
• Herniations are described by their morphology: bulge (circumferential, not a herniation), protrusion (base wider than the dome), extrusion (dome wider than the base), and sequestration (a free fragment).
  • And by their location: central, paracentral (subarticular), foraminal, and extraforaminal (far lateral).

• The posterior longitudinal ligament narrows as it descends and is hourglass-shaped in the lumbar region — strong centrally, deficient laterally.
  • The annulus is thinnest posterolaterally.
  • Together these make the posterolateral corner the path of least resistance — so most herniations are paracentral, and they strike the traversing root.

text: 3.3.2 Which root is compressed — the rule to memorise

rows: Roots exit ABOVE the same-numbered pedicle, down to C7. C8 exits between C7 and T1 (there are 8 cervical roots but 7 cervical vertebrae)
A C5–C6 disc compresses the C6 root
The L4 root exits below the L4 pedicle, through the L4–L5 foramen

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
In the lumbar spine the level of the disc does not tell you the root — the position of the herniation does.
Paracentral herniation at L4–L5 catches the root that is passing through on its way to the level below: the traversing L5 root. This is much the commonest situation.
Far lateral (extraforaminal) herniation at L4–L5 catches the root that has already left: the exiting L4 root.
So the same disc produces two different syndromes depending on where it herniates, and a patient with an L4 pattern from an L4–L5 disc is not a diagnostic error — it points to a far lateral fragment.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Most herniations resorb. Extruded and sequestrated fragments — counterintuitively the more dramatic ones — resorb more readily than contained protrusions, because exposure to the epidural vascular supply triggers an inflammatory and phagocytic response.
This is worth telling patients explicitly. It changes how a frightening MRI report is received, and it supports a non-operative course in the absence of progressive deficit or cauda equina signs.

body:
• True synovial joints with a capsule, hyaline cartilage and a synovial lining. They also contain small fibroadipose meniscoids, which have been proposed as a cause of acute locking.
  • Their orientation determines regional motion (see 1.4), and they carry roughly 20% of axial load in neutral, rising in extension.

text: 4.1.1 Innervation — the basis of medial branch blocks

body:
• Each facet joint is supplied by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus at its own level and the level above — so each joint has a dual nerve supply.
  • Therefore each medial branch must be blocked at two levels to anaesthetise one joint. This is not a technical preference; it follows directly from the anatomy.
  • In the lumbar spine the medial branch crosses the junction of the superior articular process and the transverse process, in the groove beside the mammillary process. In the cervical spine the medial branches wrap around the articular pillar waist.
  • The third occipital nerve (the superficial medial branch of the C3 dorsal ramus) supplies the C2–C3 facet joint — a well-described source of cervicogenic headache.

label: Imaging & procedures
text:
Medial branch block and radiofrequency ablation follow the dual supply rule. To treat the L4–L5 facet joint you target the L3 and L4 medial branches.
Facet-mediated pain has no reliable clinical signs — no physical examination finding, imaging appearance or pain pattern is diagnostic. A controlled diagnostic block is the only way to establish it, which is why single uncontrolled blocks have high false-positive rates.

body:
• Found only in the cervical spine (C3–C7), between the uncinate process of the vertebra below and the body above.
  • Not true synovial joints — they are clefts that develop in childhood within the lateral annulus.
  • They form the anteromedial wall of the intervertebral foramen, so uncovertebral osteophytes are a leading cause of cervical foraminal stenosis and radiculopathy.

rows: Basiocciput to sacrum, along the anterior bodies and discs. Broad and strong
Ossifies in DISH, producing flowing anterior bridging
Within the canal, along the posterior bodies. Narrows caudally, hourglass-shaped in the lumbar spine
Its lateral deficiency directs herniations posterolaterally. OPLL is an important cause of myelopathy
Lamina to lamina, within the canal posteriorly. ~80% elastin — the most elastic tissue in the body
Flexion; recoils the spine to neutral
Buckles into the canal in extension → dynamic stenosis. Hypertrophies with degeneration — a major contributor to lumbar stenosis
Between and over the spinous processes
The supraspinous ligament ends around L4, leaving the lower lumbar segments less protected in flexion
The expanded cervical supraspinous ligament, external occipital protuberance to C7
Muscle attachment and a midline surgical plane

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
The ligamentum flavum explains why stenotic patients flex. In extension it buckles inward, the disc bulges back, and the facets override — the canal and foramina narrow. In flexion the opposite happens and the canal opens.
That is the anatomy behind neurogenic claudication: symptoms on standing and walking, relieved by sitting, leaning forward, or pushing a trolley — the shopping trolley sign. It is also why stenotic patients often tolerate a bicycle better than a treadmill.
Contrast vascular claudication, which is relieved by stopping regardless of position.

body:
• Transverse ligament of the atlas — the horizontal band of the cruciate ligament, holding the dens against the anterior arch of C1. The primary stabiliser of the atlantoaxial joint.
  • Alar ligaments — from the dens to the occipital condyles; limit rotation and lateral flexion. Tested by side-bending with the head held.
  • Tectorial membrane — the cranial continuation of the PLL, covering the dens posteriorly.
  • Apical ligament — dens tip to foramen magnum; of little mechanical importance.

• A hybrid joint: the anterior third is synovial, the posterior two-thirds a syndesmosis bound by strong interosseous ligaments.
  • Motion is very small — a few degrees of nutation (sacral flexion) and counternutation.
  • Form closure comes from the wedge shape and the irregular, interlocking surfaces; force closure comes from muscle and fascia — principally the latissimus dorsi and contralateral gluteus maximus acting through the thoracolumbar fascia.
  • Innervation is variable and multisegmental (roughly L4–S3 posteriorly), which is why SIJ pain refers so widely and unpredictably.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
No single physical test diagnoses SIJ pain. The evidence supports using a cluster — typically three or more positive out of five provocation tests (distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust, Gaenslen) — and even then the reference standard is a diagnostic block.
Also remember that inflammatory sacroiliitis is a different problem entirely. Inflammatory back pain — onset under 45, insidious, better with exercise, worse with rest, night pain, morning stiffness over 30 minutes — should prompt consideration of axial spondyloarthritis, not a mechanical label.
5. The Spinal Canal and Its Contents

rows: < 13 mm suggests stenosis. The Torg–Pavlov ratio (canal : vertebral body) below 0.8 indicates congenital narrowing
< 10 mm = absolute stenosis; 10–12 mm = relative. Cross-sectional area below ~100 mm² is also used

body:
• Stenosis may be central (canal), lateral recess (subarticular, catching the traversing root) or foraminal (catching the exiting root). The three produce different patterns, and a report should specify which.
  • Congenitally short pedicles produce a developmentally narrow canal, so that a modest disc bulge causes symptoms that the same bulge would not cause in a roomier canal.

• Dura mater — the tough outer layer; the dural (thecal) sac ends at about S2.
  • Arachnoid — applied to the inner dura; the subarachnoid space contains CSF and extends to S2, which is why lumbar puncture below L2 is safe — the cord has ended but the CSF has not.
  • Pia — adherent to the cord, continuing as the filum terminale and forming the denticulate ligaments that anchor the cord laterally.
  • Epidural space — outside the dura, containing fat, the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson), and the segmental vessels. It is the target of epidural injection.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Batson’s venous plexus is valveless and communicates with the pelvic, abdominal and thoracic veins. That is the accepted anatomical explanation for the spine being such a common site of metastasis from prostate, breast, lung, kidney and thyroid — and for how pelvic infection can seed the spine.
Practically: new spinal pain in a patient with a history of malignancy is a metastasis until proven otherwise, and the thoracic spine is the commonest site.

body:
• The cord is shorter than the canal, because the vertebral column outgrows it during development.
  • In adults the conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2. At birth it lies at about L3.
  • Below the conus, the lumbar and sacral roots descend as the cauda equina within the thecal sac.
  • Cervical enlargement (C4–T1) supplies the upper limb; lumbosacral enlargement (L1–S3) supplies the lower limb.
  • The discrepancy between cord level and vertebral level widens as you descend — which is why a mid-thoracic vertebral lesion affects cord segments several levels lower.

• One anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord — including the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and the anterior horns.
  • Two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third — principally the dorsal columns. Being paired, this territory is better protected.
  • These longitudinal vessels are reinforced by segmental radiculomedullary arteries, of which the largest is the artery of Adamkiewicz — usually arising between T9 and T12, and on the left in about 75%.
  • The T4–T9 region is a vascular watershed, with the fewest reinforcing vessels.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Anterior spinal artery syndrome produces loss of motor function and of pain and temperature below the level, with preserved proprioception and vibration — because the dorsal columns have a separate, paired supply. The dissociation is the diagnostic clue.
The classic settings are aortic surgery or dissection, profound hypotension, and thoracic cord ischaemia in the T4–T9 watershed. This is also why maintaining perfusion pressure matters in acute cord injury.

rows: The pedicles of the vertebrae above and below
The vertebral bodies and the intervertebral disc (and in the neck, the uncovertebral joint)

body:
• The foramen contains the dorsal root ganglion, the ventral and dorsal roots, the sinuvertebral nerve, and radicular vessels — and the nerve occupies only about a third of it, which is why substantial narrowing is tolerated before symptoms appear.
  • The foramen narrows in extension, ipsilateral side-bending and rotation — which is precisely the combination of Spurling’s test.

label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
text:
The dorsal root ganglion sits within the foramen — and this single fact underpins electrodiagnosis of radiculopathy.
A radiculopathy is proximal to the DRG, so the sensory cell body and its peripheral axon remain intact: the sensory nerve action potential is preserved even when the patient is numb.
A plexus or peripheral nerve lesion is distal to the DRG, so the SNAP is reduced or absent.
Numbness with a normal SNAP → think root.
Numbness with a reduced SNAP → think plexus or peripheral nerve.
Add the paraspinal muscles: they are supplied by the dorsal ramus, which leaves immediately at the root level. Abnormal paraspinals are strong evidence of a root lesion; normal paraspinals do not exclude one, because they reinnervate early and are technically difficult to sample.

rows: Shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion
Ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, hip abduction, foot inversion (tib. posterior)

label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
text:
There is no reliable L5 reflex — the medial hamstring reflex is difficult to elicit and poorly reproducible. The ankle jerk is S1.
Localising an L5 lesion therefore rests on the motor examination, and three muscles do the work: tibialis posterior (L5 via the tibial nerve), gluteus medius (L5 via the superior gluteal nerve) and the peroneals (L5–S1 via the superficial fibular nerve).
All three weak, with abnormal paraspinals and a preserved SNAP → L5 radiculopathy.
Only the peroneals and dorsiflexors weak, with normal tibialis posterior and gluteus medius → common fibular neuropathy at the fibular neck.
The same logic runs in the arm: rhomboids (dorsal scapular, off the root) and serratus anterior (long thoracic, off the roots) separate a C5 root lesion from an upper trunk plexopathy.

rows: A cord lesion causes ipsilateral weakness below the level
A cord lesion causes ipsilateral loss below the level
Within 1–2 segments of entry, in the anterior commissure
A cord lesion causes CONTRALATERAL loss, beginning 1–2 levels below the lesion

label: Memory aid
text:
Two decussate high, one decussates immediately. Motor and dorsal columns cross in the medulla, so their deficits are ipsilateral to a cord lesion. Pain and temperature cross within a segment or two of entering, so that deficit is contralateral.
That single asymmetry generates the whole pattern of Brown-Séquard syndrome — and it is why the sensory level for pinprick sits one or two segments below the true lesion.

rows: Central cord and lateral corticospinal fibres; hyperextension in a stenotic canal
Arms weaker than legs, hands worst. Sacral sparing. The commonest incomplete syndrome
Anterior two-thirds — anterior spinal artery territory
Motor and pain/temperature lost; proprioception and vibration preserved. Poorest prognosis
Ipsilateral motor, proprioception and vibration loss; contralateral pain and temperature loss. Best prognosis
Loss of proprioception and vibration; sensory ataxia. Rare
Cord segments S2–S5 at L1–L2 vertebral level
Sudden, symmetrical; early and severe bladder and bowel involvement; symmetrical saddle anaesthesia; mixed UMN and LMN; less radicular pain
Gradual, asymmetrical; prominent radicular pain; LMN only (areflexia); bladder involvement is later

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Cauda equina syndrome is the spinal emergency you must not miss. Ask directly about new urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, saddle anaesthesia and bilateral leg symptoms — patients rarely volunteer them.
Retention with overflow is the most consistent finding. If suspected, examine perianal sensation and anal tone, check a post-void residual, and arrange urgent MRI — the same day. Do not wait for bilateral weakness.
The distinction from conus syndrome matters less in the acute setting than the recognition: both need urgent imaging and decompression.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Myelopathy is the diagnosis that gets missed in a spine clinic, because patients present with vague complaints: clumsy hands, dropping things, difficulty with buttons, and unsteadiness on the feet.
Examine for it deliberately in every patient with neck pain: Hoffmann’s sign, inverted supinator reflex, brisk lower limb reflexes, clonus, Babinski, and a tandem gait. Ask specifically about handwriting and buttons.
The combination that should stop you: LMN signs at the level and UMN signs below it — for example, wasted hand intrinsics with brisk knee jerks and an upgoing plantar. That is cervical myelopathy until proven otherwise.

body: The back muscles are conventionally grouped into three layers, and the division is not arbitrary — it follows the innervation.

rows: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae
Move the upper limb — they are limb muscles that happen to attach to the spine
Accessory respiratory; of little clinical importance

label: Memory aid
text: The true back muscles are the only ones in the body supplied by dorsal rami. If a muscle is supplied by a dorsal ramus, it is an intrinsic spinal muscle. That is also why paraspinal needle EMG localises to the root — the dorsal ramus leaves immediately, before any plexus forms.

body:
• A common tendinous origin from the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spinous processes, dividing into three columns.
  • Iliocostalis (lateral) · Longissimus (intermediate) · Spinalis (medial).
  • Acting bilaterally they extend the spine; unilaterally they side-bend.
  • They work largely eccentrically, controlling forward flexion rather than producing extension.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
The flexion–relaxation phenomenon. In a healthy spine, the erector spinae switch off at full forward flexion — the load is taken by the passive ligamentous system. In chronic low back pain this relaxation is lost, and the muscles remain active throughout.
It is one of the more reproducible physiological findings in chronic back pain, and a useful concept to explain to patients why their back “never switches off”.

rows: Extension and contralateral rotation; semispinalis capitis is a major neck extensor
2–4 segments; thickest in the lumbar spine
The key segmental stabiliser. Rich in muscle spindles — as much a proprioceptive organ as a mover
Very short; the highest spindle density in the body — almost certainly proprioceptive rather than prime movers

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Multifidus atrophies rapidly, selectively and segmentally after an episode of low back pain — measurable on ultrasound or MRI within days, at the symptomatic level, and it does not recover spontaneously when the pain settles.
That persistent, silent deficit is one proposed mechanism for recurrence, and it is the anatomical argument for specific motor-control retraining rather than general strengthening alone. Be honest with patients about the evidence, though: motor control exercise is effective, but not clearly superior to other forms of active exercise in trials.
Fatty infiltration of multifidus on MRI is a marker of chronicity — worth noting when you see it on a report.

body:
• Interspinales and intertransversarii — tiny, spanning one segment. Densely populated with spindles; proprioceptive.
  • Levatores costarum — transverse process to the rib below.

• Bounded by rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior and obliquus capitis inferior, with rectus capitis posterior minor medially.
  • Innervation: the suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C1).
  • Contents: the vertebral artery (in the groove on the posterior arch of C1) and the suboccipital venous plexus.
  • These muscles have an extraordinarily high spindle density and are principally proprioceptive — providing head-on-neck position sense to the vestibular and visual systems.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
A myodural bridge connects rectus capitis posterior minor to the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and the cervical dura. It is proposed as a mechanism linking suboccipital dysfunction to cervicogenic headache and to dural tension.
The suboccipital muscles’ proprioceptive role also explains cervicogenic dizziness: disturbed neck afferents conflict with vestibular and visual input. This is why deep cervical flexor training and oculomotor/proprioceptive retraining feature in cervical rehabilitation, rather than strengthening alone.

body:
• Longus colli and longus capitis, lying directly on the anterior vertebral bodies.
  • They produce craniocervical flexion (a nodding motion) and stabilise the cervical lordosis segmentally.
  • They are the cervical equivalent of multifidus: postural stabilisers that are inhibited and atrophy in neck pain, while the superficial sternocleidomastoid and scalenes become overactive.
  • The craniocervical flexion test (with a pressure biofeedback unit) assesses them and is the basis of targeted retraining.

• The thoracolumbar fascia has three layers (posterior, middle and anterior) enveloping the paraspinal muscles and the quadratus lumborum.
  • Its posterior layer receives latissimus dorsi on one side and gluteus maximus on the other, forming a diagonal sling that transfers load across the sacroiliac joint — the anatomical basis of force closure.
  • It is densely innervated, and is increasingly regarded as a pain-generating structure in its own right.
  • The canister model: the diaphragm above, the pelvic floor below, transversus abdominis in front and around, and multifidus behind. Coordinated activity of all four raises intra-abdominal pressure and stiffens the lumbar spine before limb movement occurs.

label: PM&R clinical pearl
text:
Anticipatory postural adjustment is the useful finding here: in healthy people, transversus abdominis and multifidus activate a fraction of a second BEFORE the limb moves. In people with low back pain, that anticipatory timing is delayed.
The clinical implication is about timing and coordination, not strength — which is why a patient can have a strong trunk and still poor control. It also explains why breathing pattern matters: the diaphragm is a postural muscle as well as a respiratory one, and the two roles compete under load.

rows: The most prominent cervical spinous process. T1 is often equally prominent — confirm by asking the patient to extend the neck: C7 moves forward, T1 does not
Traditionally the L4 body or L4–L5 interspace
Widely used, but accurate only to within one to two levels — and it tends to be too high, particularly in women and in the obese
Also marks the end of the dural sac
The access point for caudal epidural injection

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Do not rely on surface landmarks for level-specific procedures. Studies of Tuffier’s line consistently show clinicians misidentify the interspace by one or more levels in a substantial proportion of cases, usually erring too high.
Since the conus can sit as low as L2 in some adults, an intended L3–L4 puncture that is actually at L1–L2 risks cord injury. Use imaging guidance for anything level-critical, and use ultrasound to count from the sacrum when landmarks are unreliable.
8.2.1 Tests and what they actually load

rows: Extension, ipsilateral side-bend and rotation — narrows the foramen
Cervical radiculopathy. Specific but not sensitive
Tensions the sciatic nerve and L4–S1 roots; root excursion begins around 30–35°
Lumbar radiculopathy. Sensitive, not specific. Pain below the knee matters; back pain alone does not
Much more specific for a large disc herniation
Prone knee flexion with hip extension — tensions L2–L4
Loads the facet joints and narrows the foramen
Posterior element or foraminal source — but not diagnostic of facet pain

body:
• Radiographs — alignment, disc height, listhesis, and the pars on oblique views (the “Scottie dog”, whose collar is a pars defect). Flexion–extension views assess dynamic instability.
  • MRI — the study for neural structures, disc, marrow and soft tissue. STIR sequences reveal oedema: acute fracture, infection, and the pars stress reaction.
  • CT — bone detail, fracture, ossification (OPLL), and pseudarthrosis after fusion.
  • Modic changes describe vertebral endplate marrow signal: Type 1 oedematous (associated with active pain), Type 2 fatty, Type 3 sclerotic.

label: Pitfall — do not miss
text:
Degenerative findings on MRI are close to universal and correlate poorly with pain. In asymptomatic people, disc degeneration is present in roughly 40% at age 30 and over 90% by age 60; disc bulges and annular fissures are similarly common.
So a report describing degeneration is describing ageing, not necessarily the cause of the symptoms. Imaging is most useful when it answers a specific question raised by the history and examination — and routine early imaging in non-specific low back pain worsens outcomes, through labelling and the cascade of further investigation.
The wording you use matters: “age-related changes” conveys the same fact as “degenerative disc disease” without implying a progressive disease.
8.4 Procedures and the anatomy behind them

rows: Posterior epidural space, between adjacent laminae
Passes through the ligamentum flavum — the basis of loss of resistance
The “safe triangle” beneath the pedicle, above the exiting root

Places medication at the dorsal root ganglion and ventral epidural space. Beware the artery of Adamkiewicz and radicular arteries — the reason particulate steroid is avoided in transforaminal injections
Safe distance from the dural sac (which ends at S2), but a large volume is needed to reach the lumbar levels
Junction of the superior articular and transverse processes (lumbar); articular pillar waist (cervical)
Each facet has a dual supply, so two medial branches are targeted per joint
The inferior third of the joint — the synovial portion
Only the anteroinferior part is a true synovial joint

No reliable clinical sign — diagnosis rests on controlled blocks

Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal vertebrae
Intervertebral discs — none at C1–C2 or above
Where the conus medullaris ends in adults (L3 at birth)

body:
• Facet orientation explains regional motion. Sagittal lumbar facets permit flexion but block rotation — the lumbar spine bends well and twists badly.
  • The three-joint complex: one disc and two facets. Degenerate one and you load the others.
  • The disc is avascular and fed by diffusion driven by loading cycles — movement nourishes it, immobility starves it.
  • The PLL is deficient laterally, so herniations go posterolaterally.
  • Cervical roots exit ABOVE their pedicle; lumbar roots exit BELOW. C5–C6 disc → C6 root; L4–L5 paracentral disc → L5 root.
  • A far lateral herniation catches the exiting root, so the same disc produces a different syndrome.
  • Extruded and sequestrated discs resorb more readily than contained ones — tell patients this.
  • Each facet joint has a dual nerve supply, so two medial branches are blocked per joint.
  • Ligamentum flavum buckles in extension — the anatomy of neurogenic claudication and the shopping trolley sign.
  • The conus ends at L1–L2 but the dural sac ends at S2 — which is what makes lumbar puncture below L2 safe.
  • The DRG lies in the foramen, proximal to it → SNAPs are preserved in radiculopathy.
  • Paraspinals are supplied by dorsal rami, so abnormal paraspinals localise to the root.
  • Spinothalamic fibres cross within 1–2 segments, so the pinprick level sits below the true lesion.
  • LMN signs at the level with UMN signs below = myelopathy until proven otherwise.
  • Degenerative MRI findings are near-universal with age. Image to answer a question, not to explain pain.

• New urinary retention, saddle anaesthesia or bilateral leg symptoms → cauda equina syndrome. Same-day MRI.
  • Clumsy hands, gait unsteadiness, brisk reflexes with wasted hand intrinsics → cervical myelopathy.
  • New spinal pain in a patient with a history of cancer, or with weight loss and night pain → metastasis until proven otherwise; the thoracic spine is the commonest site.
  • Fever, rigors, intravenous drug use, recent bacteraemia or spinal procedure → discitis or epidural abscess. Inflammatory markers and MRI.
  • Sudden severe pain in an older or osteoporotic patient, or on long-term steroids → vertebral fragility fracture.
  • Inflammatory back pain — onset under 45, insidious, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, better with exercise and worse with rest → axial spondyloarthritis.
  • Thoracic pain, particularly new and in an older patient → a lower prior probability of a mechanical cause; image earlier.
  • Neck pain with any long-tract sign in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome → image the craniocervical junction before any manual treatment.
Anatomy only. Spinal biomechanics — segmental kinematics, coupled motion, load modelling and the mechanics of instability — is treated separately.
